blocks.text: The change of ruler in verses 9–10 has a near-contemporary Babylonian parallel. BM 21946 records a campaign against Judah, the capture of its king, the installation of another king, and the removal of tribute. It provides an external witness to this political transition, though it does not describe the later destruction of the temple.

sections.title: A Babylonian Record of the Transition

blocks.text: The chapter’s conclusion interprets Jerusalem’s destruction and exile through the people’s persistent rejection of God’s messengers, the desolation of the land, and Jeremiah’s word. Yet the final verses immediately open a restoration: Cyrus authorizes the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem. The movement from ruin to authorization is therefore central to the chapter’s own ending.

The seventy years in verses 20–23 echoes Jeremiah’s association of Babylonian domination and restoration with that period. Chronicles uses the number within its account of the land’s sabbath rest and the fulfillment of Jeremiah’s word; later readers continued to interpret the seventy years in different ways.

Cyrus’s proclamation is the beginning of restoration, not necessarily its complete accomplishment. Ezra 1–6 portrays a longer and contested process involving return support, temple vessels, opposition, prophetic encouragement, official inquiries, and eventual completion under Darius. A Babylonian foundation inscription known as the Cyrus Cylinder offers imperial context for restoration policies, but because it does not mention Judah or Jerusalem, it should not be treated as a copy of Cyrus’s proclamation here.
